'''whole-souled''' (hōl′sōld), ''a.'' Noble; generous; hearty.

'''whole-stitch''' (hōl′stich), ''n.'' In lace, the simplest kind of filling, in which the threads are woven together, as in cloth.

'''wholly''' (hō′li), ''adv.'' [With unorig. ''w'', as in ''whole''; prop. ''holely'' or ''holly'', < ME. ''holely'', ''hoolli'', ''holly'', ''holli'', ''holliche''; < ''whole'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' Entirely; completely; perfectly; without reserve.
{{smaller block|Sleep hath seized me ''wholly''. ''Shak.'', Cymbeline, ii. 2. 7.

To her my life I ''wholly'' sacrifice.
{{right|''Spenser'', Colin Clout, l. 475.}}}}
'''2.''' Altogether; exclusively; only.
{{smaller block|Arthur seide, “I put me ''holly'' in God and in holy cherche, and in youre gode counseile.” ''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 104.

A bully thinks honour consists ''wholly'' in being brave.
{{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 217.}}}}

'''wholth''' (hōlth), ''n.'' [< ''whole'' + ''-th''; intended to explain the lit. sense of ''health''.] Wholeness; soundness; health. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|That “perfect diapason” which constitutes health, or ''wholth'', and for the use or abuse of which he, as a rational being, is answerable on soul and conscience to himself, to his fellow-men, and to his Maker.
{{right|''Dr. J. Brown'', Spare Hours, 3d ser., p. 125.}}}}

'''whom''' (höm), ''pron.'' The objective case (original dative) of ''who''.

'''whomever''' (höm-ev′ėr), ''pron.'' The objective case of ''whoever''.

'''whommle, whomble''' (hwom′l, hwom′bl), ''v. t.'' Dialectal forms of ''whemmle.''
{{smaller block|I think I see the coble ''whombled'' keel up.
{{right|''Scott'', Antiquary, xl.}}
''Whommle'', “to turn a trough, or any vessel, bottom upwards, so that it will drain well”: used in West Virginia.
{{right|''Trans. Amer. Philol. Ass.'', XIV. 55.}}}}

'''whomso''' (höm′sō), ''pron.'' The objective case of ''whoso.''

'''whomsoever''' (höm′sọ̄-ev′ėr), ''pron.'' The objective case of ''whosoever.''

'''whoobub†''' (hö′bub), ''n.'' Another spelling of ''whobub.''
{{smaller block|Had not the old man come in with a ''whoo-bub'' against his daughter.
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., iv. 4. 629.}}}}

'''whoop<sup>1</sup>''' (höp), ''v.'' [Properly, as formerly, ''hoop'', the initial ''w'' being unoriginal, as in ''whole'', etc., and the proper pron. being höp (as given in Walker), and not hwöp, which, so far as it exists, is a perverted pronunciation, prob. due to the spelling; < ME. ''houpen, howpen, whowpen'', < OF. ''houper'', whoop, shout; cf. ''houp!'' interj., ''houp-la!'' stop! stop there! Cf. ''hoop''<sup>2</sup>, ''hubbub'', ''whoobub.'' There may have been some connection with AS. ''wōp'', outcry, weeping (mod. E. *''woop''), Goth. ''wōpjan'', crow as a cock, etc. (see ''weep''); but none with Goth. ''hwōpjan'', boast.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To shout with a loud voice; cry out loudly, as in excitement, or in calling to some one; halloo; shout; also, to hoot, as an owl.
{{smaller block|Hit fill that thei mette Merlin with the Dragon in his hande that com hem a-geins; and as soone as he saugh hem comynge he gan to ''whowpe.''
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 353.}}}}

Eng.]—'''A lie out of whole cloth.''' See ''lie''<sup>2</sup>.—'''In or with a whole skin.''' See ''skin''.—'''The whole box and dice.''' See ''dice''<sup>3</sup>.—'''The whole kit.''' See ''kit''<sup>3</sup>.—'''The whole world.''' See ''world''.—'''To go the whole figure, the whole hog.''' See ''go''.—'''Upon the whole matter.''' See ''matter''.—'''Whole blood, culverin, curvature.''' See the nouns.—'''Whole cadence.''' Same as ''perfect cadence'' (which see, under ''cadence'').—'''Whole chest.''' See ''tea-chest''.—'''Whole cradle,''' in ''mining'', a platform suspended in the shaft, and nearly as large as the shaft itself: such a platform or cradle is hung by chains to a crab-rope let down from the surface, and is used for repairs, etc.—'''Whole deal.''' See ''deal''<sup>2</sup>, 1.—'''Whole flat,''' in working coal by the panel or barrier system, a whole panel, or such a portion of a seam as is distinctly separated from the rest by a barrier. [North. Eng.]—'''Whole milk.''' See ''milk''.—'''Whole number,''' an integer, as opposed to a fraction.—'''Whole press,''' hand-presswork done by two men, one to ink and one to print.—'''Whole shift.''' See ''shift'', 2.—'''Whole sine of a circle,''' the radius.—'''Whole stalls,''' in ''mining'', a certain number of stalls of which the faces are on a line with each other. [South Wales coal-field.]—'''Whole step.''' See ''step'', 14.—'''Whole tone.''' See ''tone''<sup>1</sup>, 5. ='''Syn. 4''' and '''5.''' ''Entire, Total,'' etc. See ''complete''.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' An entire thing; a thing complete in itself; the entire or total assemblage of parts; all of a thing without defect or exception.
{{smaller block|It was not safe to leave him [Edward II.] a Part, by which he might afterward recover the ''whole''.
{{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 112.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>’Tis not the ''whole'' of life to live,
Nor all of death to die.</poem>
{{right|''Montgomery'', Oh, where shall rest be found?}}}}
{{smaller block|But, bad though they nearly all are as ''wholes'', his [Dryden’s] plays contain passages which only the great masters have surpassed.
{{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 1st ser., p. 59.}}}}
'''2.''' A complete system; a regular combination of parts; an organic unity.
{{smaller block|<poem>All are but parts of one stupendous ''whole'',
Whose body Nature is, and God the soul.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Essay on Man, i. 267.}}}}
{{smaller block|Nature is not an aggregate of independent parts, but an organic ''whole''.
{{right|''Tyndall'', Radiation, § 16.}}}}
'''Actual whole.''' {{smaller|See ''actual''.}}—'''By the whole†''', wholesale.
{{smaller block|If the currier bought not leather ''by the whole'' of the tanner, the shoemaker might have it at a more reasonable price.
{{right|''Greene'', Quip for an Upstart Courtier (Harl. Misc., V. 411).}}}}
'''Collective, composite, constituent, constituted whole.''' {{smaller|See the adjectives.}}—'''Committee of the whole.''' {{smaller|See ''committee''.}}—'''Definitive, dissimilar, essential, formal, logical, mathematical, metaphysical, natural whole.''' {{smaller|See the adjectives.}}—'''On''' or '''upon the whole''', {{smaller|all circumstances being considered or balanced against one another; upon a review of the whole matter.}}
{{smaller block|''Upon the whole'', I do not know but he is most fortunate who engages in the whirl through ambition, however tormenting.
{{right|''Irving''. (''Imp. Dict.'')}}}}
{{smaller block|The death of Elizabeth, though ''on the whole'' it improved Bacon’s prospects, was in one respect an unfortunate event for him.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Lord Bacon.}}}}
'''Physical, positive, potential whole.''' See the adjectives. ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|Total, totality, entirety, amount, aggregate, gross, sum.}}

'''whole†''' (hōl), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''hool''; < ''whole'', ''a.'' (prop. the adj. in predicate use).]   Wholly; entirely.
{{smaller block|Therfore I aske yow counseile how we may beste be gouerned, ffor I putte me all ''hooll'' in youre ordenaunce.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 317.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The Ills thou dost are ''whole'' thine own,
Thou’rt Principal and Instrument.</poem>
{{right|''Cowley'', The Mistress, The Innocent, iii.}}}}
'''whole-colored''' (hōl′kul″ọrd), ''a.'' All of one color; unicolorous; concolor: opposed to ''party-colored.''

'''whole-footed''' (hōl′fu̇t″ed), ''a.''   [< ME. ''hole-foted''; < ''whole'' + ''footed.'']   '''1†.''' Web-footed.
{{smaller block|The ''hole foted'' fowle to the flod hyȝez.
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), ii. 538.}}}}
'''2.''' Heavy-footed.   ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]—'''3.''' Unreserved; frank; free; easy; at ease; intimate. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|His chief Remissions were when some of his nearest Relations were with him, or he with them, and then, as they say, he was ''whole-footed''; but this was not often, nor long together.
{{right|''Roger North'', quoted in N. and Q., 7th ser., I. 447.}}}}

'''whole-hoofed''' (hōl′höft), ''a.'' Having undivided hoofs; solidungulate.

'''whole-length''' (hōl′length), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Extending from end to end.—'''2.''' Of full length; exhibiting the whole figure.
{{smaller block|John Closterman was the artist who painted the ''whole-length'' portrait of Queen Anne now in the Guildhall.
{{right|''J. Ashton'', Social Life in Reign of Queen Anne, II. 45.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' A portrait or statue exhibiting the whole figure.

'''wholeness''' (hōl′nes), ''n.'' The state of being whole, complete, entire, or sound; entireness; totality; completeness.
{{smaller block|There never can be that actual ''wholeness'' of the world for us which there must be for the mind that renders the world one.
{{right|''T. H. Green'', Prolegomena to Ethics, § 72.}}}}

note rest. See ''rest''<sup>1</sup>, 3 (''b'').

'''wholesale''' (hōl′sāl), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [< ''whole'' + ''sale''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''n.'' Sale of goods by the piece or in large quantity, as distinguished from ''retail.''—'''By wholesale''' {{smaller|(or, elliptically, '''wholesale'''), in the mass; in the gross; in great quantities; hence, without due discrimination or distinction.}}
{{smaller block|And are those fit to correct the Church that are not fit to come into it? Besides, What makes them fly out upon the Function, and rail ''by wholesale?'' Is the Priesthood a crime, and the service of God a Disadvantage?
{{right|''Jeremy Collier'', Short View (ed. 1698), p. 139.}}}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Buying and selling by the piece or in large quantity: as, a ''wholesale'' dealer.—'''2.''' Pertaining to the trade by the piece or quantity: as, the ''wholesale'' price.—'''3.''' Figuratively, in great quantities; extensive and indiscriminate: as, ''wholesale'' slaughter.

'''wholesale''' (hōl′sāl), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''wholesaled'', ppr. ''wholesaling''.   [< ''wholesale'', ''n.'']   To sell by wholesale or in large quantities.

'''wholesaler''' (hōl′sā-lėr), ''n.''   [< ''wholesale'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who sells by wholesale; a wholesale merchant.
{{smaller block|Articles which the consumer recognizes as single the retailer keeps wrapped up in dozens, the ''wholesaler'' sends the gross, and the manufacturer supplies in packages of a hundred gross.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Biol., § 176.}}}}

'''whole-skinned''' (hōl′skind), ''a.'' Having the skin unbroken; sound; uninjured.
{{smaller block|He is ''whole skinn’d'', has no hurt yet.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Rule a Wife, i. 1.}}}}

'''whole-snipe''' (hōl′snīp), ''n.'' The common snipe, ''Gallinago media'' or ''G. cœlestis'', of Europe: so called in distinction from ''double-snipe'' and ''half-snipe'' (see these words).

'''wholesome''' (hōl′sum), ''a.''   [With unorig. ''w'', as in ''whole''; prop., as in early mod. E., ''holesome''; < ME. ''holsom'', ''holsum'', ''helsum'', ''halsum'', wholesome, salutary (not in AS.); prob. suggested by Icel. ''heilsamr'', wholesome, salutary, < ''heill'', = E. ''whole'', + ''-samr'' = E. ''-some'': see ''whole'' and ''-some''.]   '''1.''' Healthy; whole; sound in mind or body. [Obsolescent.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Like a mildew’d ear
Blasting his ''wholesome'' brother.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 4. 65.}}}}
{{smaller block|The purifying influence scattered throughout the atmosphere of the household by the presence of one youthful, fresh, and thoroughly ''wholesome'' heart.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, ix.}}}}
'''2.''' Tending to promote health; favoring health; healthful; salubrious: as, ''wholesome'' air or diet; a ''wholesome'' climate.
{{smaller block|Or well of Helesey, whose waters, bycause they were bytter salt, and bareyne, ye sayd prophet helyd them and made them swete and ''holsome.''
{{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 53.}}}}
{{smaller block|I did commend the black-oppressing humour to the most ''wholesome'' physic of thy health-giving air.
{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., i. 1. 235.}}}}
{{smaller block|The soile is not very fertile, subiect to much snow, the aire ''holesome.'' {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 523.}}}}
'''3.''' Contributing to health of mind or character; favorable mentally or morally; sound; salutary: as, ''wholesome'' advice; ''wholesome'' doctrines; ''wholesome'' truths. {{smaller block|But to find citizens ruled by good and ''wholesome'' laws, that is an exceeding rare and hard thing!
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), i.}}}}
{{smaller block|I find it ''wholesome'' to be alone the greater part of the time.
{{right|''Thoreau'', Walden, p. 147.}}}}
{{smaller block|With a ''wholesome'' fear of Burke and Debrett before my eyes, I suppress the proper name of the noble maiden.
{{right|''Whyte Melville'', Good for Nothing, i. 1.}}}}
'''4†.''' Profitable; advantageous; hence, prosperous.
{{smaller block|When shalt thou see thy ''wholesome'' days again?
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iv. 3. 105.}}}}
'''5.''' Clean and neat. [Now only prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|For, how Negligent soever People may be at Home, yet when they come before their Betters ’tis Manners to look ''wholsom.''
{{right|''Jeremy Collier'', Short View (ed. 1698), p. 22.}}}}
='''Syn.''' {{smaller|''Salutary'', etc. (see ''healthy''), nourishing, nutritious, invigorating, beneficial.}}

'''wholesomely''' (hōl′sum-li), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''holsumly, holsumliche''; < ''wholesome'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.]   In a wholesome or salutary manner; healthfully.
{{smaller block|The hende knyȝt at home ''holsumly'' slepe
With-inne the comly cortynes, on the colde morne.
{{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1732.}}}}
{{smaller block|Consideration for his wife seemed a ''wholesomely'' pervasive feeling with him.
{{right|''Scribner’s Mag.'', IV. 749.}}}}

'''wholesomeness''' (hōl′sum-nes), ''n.''   [< ME. ''holsumnesse''; < ''wholesome'' + ''-ness.'']   '''1.''' The quality of being wholesome or of contributing to health; salubrity. {{smaller block|Description, but also of a perfect constitution of body.
{{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, I. 108.}}}}
'''2.''' Salutariness; conduciveness to mental, moral, or social health.

'''whole-souled''' (hōl′sōld), ''a.'' Noble; generous; hearty.

'''whole-stitch''' (hōl′stich), ''n.'' In lace, the simplest kind of filling, in which the threads are woven together, as in cloth.

'''wholly''' (hō′li), ''adv.''   [With unorig. ''w'', as in ''whole''; prop. ''holely'' or ''holly'', < ME. ''holely'', ''hoolli'', ''holly'', ''holli'', ''holliche''; < ''whole'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''1.''' Entirely; completely; perfectly; without reserve.
{{smaller block|Sleep hath seized me ''wholly''. ''Shak.'', Cymbeline, ii. 2. 7.

To her my life I ''wholly'' sacrifice.
{{right|''Spenser'', Colin Clout, l. 475.}}}}
'''2.''' Altogether; exclusively; only.
{{smaller block|Arthur seide, “I put me ''holly'' in God and in holy cherche, and in youre gode counseile.” ''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 104.

A bully thinks honour consists ''wholly'' in being brave.
{{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 217.}}}}

'''wholth''' (hōlth), ''n.''   [< ''whole'' + ''-th''; intended to explain the lit. sense of ''health''.]   Wholeness; soundness; health. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|That “perfect diapason” which constitutes health, or ''wholth'', and for the use or abuse of which he, as a rational being, is answerable on soul and conscience to himself, to his fellow-men, and to his Maker.
{{right|''Dr. J. Brown'', Spare Hours, 3d ser., p. 125.}}}}

'''whom''' (höm), ''pron.'' The objective case (original dative) of ''who''.

'''whomever''' (höm-ev′ėr), ''pron.'' The objective case of ''whoever''.

'''whommle, whomble''' (hwom′l, hwom′bl), ''v. t.'' Dialectal forms of ''whemmle.''
{{smaller block|I think I see the coble ''whombled'' keel up.
{{right|''Scott'', Antiquary, xl.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Whommle'', “to turn a trough, or any vessel, bottom upwards, so that it will drain well”: used in West Virginia.
{{right|''Trans. Amer. Philol. Ass.'', XIV. 55.}}}}

'''whomso''' (höm′sō), ''pron.'' The objective case of ''whoso.''

'''whomsoever''' (höm′sọ̄-ev′ėr), ''pron.'' The objective case of ''whosoever.''

'''whoobub†''' (hö′bub), ''n.'' Another spelling of ''whobub.''
{{smaller block|Had not the old man come in with a ''whoo-bub'' against his daughter.
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., iv. 4. 629.}}}}

'''whoop<sup>1</sup>''' (höp), ''v.''   [Properly, as formerly, ''hoop'', the initial ''w'' being unoriginal, as in ''whole'', etc., and the proper pron. being höp (as given in Walker), and not hwöp, which, so far as it exists, is a perverted pronunciation, prob. due to the spelling; < ME. ''houpen, howpen, whowpen'', < OF. ''houper'', whoop, shout; cf. ''houp!'' interj., ''houp-la!'' stop! stop there! Cf. ''hoop''<sup>2</sup>, ''hubbub'', ''whoobub.'' There may have been some connection with AS. ''wōp'', outcry, weeping (mod. E. *''woop''), Goth. ''wōpjan'', crow as a cock, etc. (see ''weep''); but none with Goth. ''hwōpjan'', boast.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To shout with a loud voice; cry out loudly, as in excitement, or in calling to some one; halloo; shout; also, to hoot, as an owl.
{{smaller block|Hit fill that thei mette Merlin with the Dragon in his hande that com hem a-geins; and as soone as he saugh hem comynge he gan to ''whowpe.''
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 353.}}}}

{{smaller block|I ''whoope'', I call. . . . ''Whooppe'' a lowde, and thou shalte here hym blow his horne.
{{right|''Palsgrave'', p. 781.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Gaules stood upon the banke with disstant ''hooping'', hollaing, yelling, and singing, after their manner.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Livy, p. 408.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Sometimes they ''whoop'', sometimes their Stygian cries
Send their black Santos to the blushing skies.</poem>
{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, i. 10.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''med.'', to make a sonorous inspiration, as that following the paroxysm of coughing in whooping-cough.

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To hoot at; insult or deride with shouts or hooting; drive or follow with shouts or outcry.
{{smaller block|<poem>Suffer’d me by the voice of slaves to be
''Whoop’d'' out of Rome.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., iv. 5. 84.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>If we complain, . . .
We are mad straight, and ''whoop’d'', and tied in fetters.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher and Rowley'', Maid in the Mill, iii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I should be hissed,
And ''whooped'' in hell for that ingratitude.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Don Sebastian, ii. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' To call or signal to by a shout or whoop.—{{smaller|'''To whoop it up''', to raise an outcry or disturbance; hence, to hurry or stir matters up; work in a lively, rousing manner. [Slang.]}}
{{smaller block|His rival is a prominent politician, with an abundance of party workers to ''whoop it up'' for him.
{{right|''The Century'', XXXVIII. 156.}}}}

'''whoop<sup>1</sup>''' (höp), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''hoop'', ''howp'': see ''whoop''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' A whooping or hoot-<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
